newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria Socialist congress to discuss crisis plan.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria Socialist congress to discuss crisis plan.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists meet this weekend for a communist-style party congress, promising to resolve their internal differences and draw up an action plan to tackle the country's economic crisis.

Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, under pressure to show he is taking real steps to ward off further economic collapse, promised the congress last month after 19 prominent Socialists signed a letter calling for a new cabinet and policy reforms.

Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) deputy leader Georgi Parvanov promised the two-day meeting which opens on Saturday would not be a rubber stamp affair. "The congress will take strong political decisions," he told reporters.
Most commentators expect a cabinet reshuffle but say Videnov will probably remain as prime minister.

"A positive outcome would be a mandate for a currency board and structural reforms, though I'm not sure how persuasive it would be," said one diplomat. "The government hasn't shown much inclination for reform so far."

Videnov said on December 9 the government planned a package of stabilisation measures to accompany introduction of a currency board, under which levs in circulation must be matched by central bank reserves.
The government has been slow to deliver on previous promises of structural reform.
Economists warn that a lev peg alone will not solve Bulgaria's problems unless it is accompanied by a serious commitment to reform measures delayed in the seven years since the end of one-party rule.
The government's critics note that the congress coincides with the start of a four day public holiday, which will divert public attention.

The main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) says a currency board would fail under the present government and has called for the replacement of the central bank's directors, who would implement the mechanism, and for early general elections.
Economists say speed is of the essence if further economic collapse is to be averted and the UDF proposal would just delay the process further.

Attacks on Videnov's government, which is half way through its four-year term, became more vocal after the Socialist candidate's resounding defeat in last month's presidential election. A marathon 20-hour party plenum last month gave Videnov only narrow backing in a confidence vote.
Foreign Minister Georgi Pirinski, a prominent critic of the prime minister, resigned the following day, saying the government did not have enough support to continue ruling.
Videnov has not yet presented Pirinski's resignation to parliament.
Three members of the party's executive bureau resigned at the plenum, including vice chairman Yanaki Stoilov.
The BSP was formed by leading communists who hastily renamed themselves socialists after the fall of hardline leader Todor Zhivkov in 1989.

Andrei Raichev, a leading member of the party's reformist Union for Social Democracy wing, said the economic crisis had reinforced the party's neo-Communist tendencies, making it harder for them to surrender the principle of state ownership.

"They see more or less Communist measures as a last chance," he told Reuters. "They are not against democracy, they are not against elections, but they believe that the state can work miracles, that it can be a superpower which will solve all their problems."
